summary: Mechanism is real in master's code: consume_item runs both consumer warpgroups in lockstep with variant A's wgmma_wait<0>, so the dequant and the 16 wgmmas serialize. The in-prepare exact-compare and interleaved A/B against master's own rega make a single scored run interpretable without a companion. The biggest threat to the first_turn target is an L2-to-SM ingest ceiling, not correctness. Keep it separate from producer-scale-expand; build a stack only later, as a third gated kernel.
justification: A. The mechanism checks out against submission.py. consume_item (~line 2693) does mbar_wait(full) -> dq_stage -> 8 register-A wgmma -> commit -> wgmma_wait<0> -> arrive(empty). Both warpgroups (cw 0-3 = rows 0-63, cw 4-7 = rows 64-127) walk the same n with no offset, so per SM the tensor core idles during both groups' dequant, and the ALUs idle while 2 x 8 m64nNBk16 issue back to back. At NB=128, 2 x 8 x 131K FMA / ~2048 FMA/clk/SM = 1024 clk per stage of pure MMA. The profile's first_turn rega rows (w13 3556-3851 us, w2 1848-1925 us across the four first_turn shapes in FINDINGS) give the stated ~1530 clk/stage at ~30.5K local routes. That leaves ~500 clk that matches one serialized dequant of 2 warps per SMSP x ~180 instructions plus smem latency. Moving the two warpgroups half a stage apart with named barriers 2/3 is the standard CUTLASS ping-pong idea, and it keeps variant A inside each warpgroup, so there is no new register-A hazard. Outputs are bit-identical by construction: the per-warpgroup accumulation order is unchanged, so an exactness gate of max diff == 0 is a sound, cheap proof. I hand-simulated the barrier counts with KS=32 for 0, 1 and 2 items per CTA. With 0 items there are no PP ops. With 1 item WG1 does 31 in-loop PP_A syncs plus 1 final = 32, against WG2's 32 PP_A arrives, and 32 PP_B arrives against 32 syncs. With 2 items it is 64/64. WG2 cannot arrive PP_A twice in one phase, because its next PP_B sync needs WG1's next arrive, which follows WG1's PP_A sync. The epilogue's named_bar(1,256) cannot deadlock against PP: WG2 reaches bar 1 after its last PP_B sync, which WG1 has already satisfied. The expected directions fit the shape weights: the sliding first_turn shape (weight 138) carries most of the gain, turn_4 at bucket 128/64 gets a smaller share, and turn_1 at buckets 32/64 (~42 routes/expert, mostly NB=64, 256 clk of MMA per stage for both groups) has little MMA to hide behind, so flat there is correctly allowed. WEAKEST LINK: the claim that the ~500 exposed clk/stage are dequant serialization rather than L2->SM ingest. Each stage moves 41,984 B per CTA (9216 weight + 2 x 16 KB activation slab at NB=128). 132 CTAs at ~1530 clk/stage is already ~6.3-6.5 TB/s of L2->SM traffic at ~1.75-1.85 GHz. The 1024-clk ideal needs ~9.5 TB/s, and the w13 <= 3100 us target needs ~7.6 TB/s. Both are at or above what H100 L2 usually delivers to SMs without cluster multicast. So the first_turn gain may be capped at ~1300 clk/stage (w13 ~3200-3300 us) or come out flat. The hypothesis names this in its Risk section, but its per-kernel print gives TFLOP/s only. It should also print achieved L2->SM bytes/s (KS x stage bytes x items / kernel time), so that a flat first_turn reads as 'ingest-capped' (which hands the problem to bm256-wide-tile) rather than as 'mechanism wrong'. Secondary weak point: the arithmetic rests on route counts backed out from floors, not measured. The prepare gate's own per-kernel timings at the gate T fix that, as long as the route count used for TFLOP/s is computed from n_padded/sorted_ids in prepare.
confounders: experts-turn-rega-s4-port-t4096: introduced rega_kernel with variant A (wgmma_wait<0> right after commit). PP's entire headroom is the serialization variant A creates. A gain measures 'PP vs variant-A lockstep', not ping-pong vs a well-pipelined baseline. Because the A/B is in-prepare against this exact kernel, this does not confound the measurement, only how far it generalizes.

experts-turn-rega-s4-first-turn-n128: the BIG (ft) class reads the block-expert table via __ldg from global and owns the first_turn rows where most of the expected gain lies. PP is tested on exactly this kernel at the T=16384 soft gate, so there is no confound, but the ft gate distribution (soft) must match what master's ft gate uses, as the hypothesis states.

align-two-phase-all-t-rega: sets chunking, item count and CTA load balance (including CTAs with zero items in the low class, which the no-PP-op guard must handle). PP changes per-stage time roughly uniformly, so it interacts with tail balance only marginally, and the in-prepare A/B runs on the same align. Not a confounder of the measurement; it is the reason the 0-item guard is mandatory.
stack-tonight-five-prefill / sglang-pipeline-parity / hybrid / Triton-line landings: they do not touch rega_kernel's consumer schedule or its memory traffic. No confound.

(not landed, but relevant) experts-rega-low-class-two-ctas-per-sm: also hides consumer dequant latency, at turn_1. If it is ever landed, it and PP would substitute for each other in the low class. PP's low-class result is valid only for the 1-CTA/SM master.
interference: No companion is warranted. The change carries its own control: prepare() runs master's rega and the PP kernel on identical routings with an exact compare (max diff 0), then cold-L2 graph medians over REGA_ALTERNATIONS interleaved alternations at each class's gate T, and turns PP ON per class only at <= 0.98x. It prints per-class PATH CHOSEN lines and per-kernel w13/w2 timings for both variants. The scored profile's rega_kernel<*,true>/<*,false> rows then show what the judge saw. That makes every outcome readable from this one run. Headline gain with PP ON means attributed to PP. Flat with PP OFF means the gate refused it, and the per-kernel prints say by how much. Flat with PP ON and ~560 TFLOP/s per kernel means the ingest-capped reading, provided the bytes/s print is added. A loss with PP ON would be a gate-vs-judge discrepancy that the profile rows show directly. An ab-revert of any landed hypothesis would not disambiguate anything the in-prepare A/B leaves open, and a control run isolating a sub-change is meaningless because PP is a single change. Spending a second scored run is not justified. On the sibling experts-rega-producer-scale-expand-all-t: KEEP SEPARATE for now. (1) Both specify the same module name muse_prefill_rega_v3 and the same 'append after _REGA_BODY' slot, and both rewrite the consumer stage loop, so a naive stack is a merge conflict, not a sum. (2) The mechanisms overlap at first_turn: SX shortens the very dequant PP tries to hide. If PP hides it fully, SX adds ~0 there, and if the kernel is ingest-capped, neither moves, so a stacked headline could not say which one mattered. (3) They are complementary mostly at turn_1, where SX targets issue count and PP has little MMA to hide behind. (4) A stack is a third kernel (PP barriers plus the sfull wait in one consumer). It needs its own exactness gate, and it adds a further ~4 instantiations of nvcc time to a prepare that already holds master's ft-start (150 s) and copy (255 s) deadlines. Read both results, then mint a depends_on-both combo kernel gated against the better single variant, and only for the classes where each showed a per-kernel win. If scored submits are so scarce that only one run is possible, the fallback is a single build carrying both variants as separate per-class options (master | pp | sx, best chosen per class, no combined kernel). That stays attributable from the prepare prints, but it costs ~8 extra instantiations of compile time.
rules_flags: No rule violation in the change as written: weights stay NVFP4/E4M3 in global memory and are dequantized in registers, bf16 activations, fp32 accumulation, every route computed, no input-derived caching, kernel_fn dispatches only on T and prepare flags, and in-process load_inline only.

Operational, not a rule, but it costs a scored submit: named barriers have no timeout, so a PP count bug hangs the GPU inside prepare(). The 'OFF: <reason>' fallback cannot catch a hang, and the run is charged as a timeout at 15 minutes. Implementation checklist: the 'first k-stage of the launch' skip must be a per-thread register flag. The final PP_A sync must be conditional on the CTA having consumed >= 1 k-stage, using the same predicate for all 128 WG1 threads. Every PP op must run on the mbar 'dead' path. Barrier IDs 2/3 must not be used anywhere else in rega_kernel_pp (0 = __syncthreads, 1 = epilogue). All 32 lanes of every consumer warp must execute each bar.sync/bar.arrive converged, so keep the lane==0 mbar_arrive outside the bar ops.

Prepare budget: v3 compiles master's source plus 4 PP instantiations in one module. The extra nvcc time lands BEFORE master's own rega checks, which are bound by REGA_FT_START_DEADLINE_S = 150 s and REGA_COPY_DEADLINE_S = 255 s inside a 300 s prepare. If the build pushes master's ft check past 150 s, master's ft rega turns OFF and first_turn regresses badly. Print elapsed time at each phase, run every PP phase strictly after master's checks under its own skip deadline, and make sure a v3 build failure falls back to master's v2 within the budget.
open_questions: What L2->SM bytes/s does master's ft rega already reach (stage bytes x k-stages / kernel time)? If it is already ~6.5 TB/s, how much ping-pong headroom exists before the ingest ceiling? Add this print next to TFLOP/s in the per-kernel lines.

Is the ~1530 clk/stage figure net of the per-item epilogue (~131 items per CTA at first_turn, ~28 us each)? The epilogue's named_bar(1,256) re-aligns the pair every item, adding a half-stage drain per item (~1.5% at KS=32). Is that accounted for in the targets?

At turn_4 (~173 routes/expert, a mix of NB=128 and NB=64 chunks), does PP win on the NB=64 items, where each group's MMA (~256 clk) is about as long as its dequant? The per-class gate decides, but a per-bucket split in the print would say whether a bucket-gated PP is the follow-up.

Is the route count used for the TFLOP/s print measured in prepare (from n_padded / sorted_ids at the gate routing) or backed out from TASK.md floors? Only the measured number makes the per-kernel efficiency comparable across variants and shapes.
